extra.message: Hardcoded Default Secrets (JWT Secret Key and Database Credentials) — JWT token forgery (impersonate any user) and unauthorized database access if defaults are used in production. [verified: config.py line 14 defaults SECRET_KEY to 'local-dev-change-me' (used by security.py to sign all JWTs) and line 12 defaults DATABASE_URL to 'postgresql+psycopg://dispatch:dispatch@localhost:5432/dispatch_ops'; no startup guard validates, warns, or rejects these defaults, so a deployment omitting the env vars runs with publicly known credentials enabling JWT forgery and database compromise.]

Hardcoded default JWT secret key enables token forgery — An attacker can forge JWTs for any user (including ops_admin) if the SECRET_KEY env var is not set, gaining full administrative access to the application and all its data. [verified: Same default JWT secret 'local-dev-change-me' at config.py line 14 is used directly by security.py jwt.encode() and jwt.decode(); no startup check across the entire codebase prevents deployment with this known default, enabling complete authentication bypass via forged JWTs.]

Path Traversal / Arbitrary File Read in ops parcel endpoint — Arbitrary file read from the server filesystem, exposing secrets, database files, source code, and system files. [verified: User-controlled `packet_ref` is joined to `BASE_EXPORT_DIR` via `BASE_EXPORT_DIR / packet_ref` on line 26 with no path sanitization, then read with `.read_text()`, enabling directory traversal to arbitrary files. The token gate is authentication only.]

Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) in ops relay endpoint — Access to internal network services, cloud metadata endpoints, and local file reads via file:// scheme. [verified: User-controlled `url` parameter is passed directly to `urllib.request.urlopen(url)` on line 32 with no scheme/host validation, allowing access to internal services and cloud metadata. Authentication does not constrain the URL target.]

Log Injection with Bearer Token Exposure in ops wire endpoint — Log forgery/poisoning and exposure of valid Authorization bearer tokens in application logs. [verified: The entire request body and Authorization header are logged at WARNING level on line 53 via `logger.warning("ops tally body=%s bearer=%s", body, request.headers.get("authorization"))`, leaking bearer tokens into logs and enabling log-forgery via newline injection. Token exposure directly undermines the ops gate.]

Code Injection via eval() in ops formula endpoint — Arbitrary Python code execution on the server, leading to full system compromise. [verified: User-controlled `expr` parameter is passed to `eval()` on line 55 with only `__builtins__` disabled — sandbox escapes via `().__class__.__bases__[0].__subclasses__()` are well-known. The internal token gate authenticates but does not validate or restrict the evaluated expression.]

Sensitive data (Authorization header) written to application logs — Bearer tokens, API keys, or other credentials sent in the Authorization header are exposed in application logs, accessible to anyone with log access [verified: The Authorization header value is logged at WARNING level on line 53 (`logger.warning(..., request.headers.get("authorization"))`), exposing bearer tokens in application logs accessible to anyone with log access.]

Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) in ops Jinja endpoint — Remote code execution on the server via Jinja2 template injection, allowing full system compromise. [verified: User-controlled `fragment` query parameter is concatenated directly into a Jinja2 Template string with no sanitization on line 82 (`Template("Result: " + fragment).render()`), enabling SSTI and potential RCE. The `_wrk_gate` token check is authentication, not input validation, and does not neutralize the injection.]

Server-Side Template Injection via Jinja2 in /ops/jinja — Attacker with internal token executes arbitrary code on the server via Jinja2 SSTI, gaining full system access [verified: Same SSTI as finding 0: user-controlled `fragment` is concatenated into `Template("Result: " + fragment).render()` on line 82 with no sanitization, enabling Jinja2 template injection and RCE.]

Path traversal in /ops/dock file write — Attacker with internal token writes arbitrary files to the server filesystem, enabling code execution or data destruction [verified: Same path traversal write as finding 10: `name` joined to `BASE_EXPORT_DIR` on line 90 without sanitization, allowing arbitrary file write via `target.write_bytes(body)`.]

Unrestricted File Write with Path Traversal in ops dock endpoint — Arbitrary file write anywhere on the filesystem, enabling code execution via webshell, cron job, or SSH key overwrite. [verified: User-controlled `name` parameter is joined to `BASE_EXPORT_DIR` on line 90 (`target = BASE_EXPORT_DIR / name`) with no path sanitization, and the full request body is written via `target.write_bytes(body)`, enabling arbitrary file write via directory traversal.]

XML External Entity injection in /ops/xml endpoint — Attacker with internal token reads local files or performs SSRF via crafted XML with external entities [verified: Same XXE as finding 4: `XMLParser(resolve_entities=True, load_dtd=True, no_network=False)` on line 96 enables external entity resolution on attacker-supplied XML body.]

NoSQL Injection in ops MongoDB endpoint — Bypass query filters to access unauthorized data, potential JavaScript execution on MongoDB server. [verified: User-supplied JSON `filter` field (or entire payload) is passed directly to `find_one(query)` on line 109 without sanitization, allowing MongoDB operator injection (`$where`, `$regex`, `$ne`). The `_wrk_gate` provides no query-level protection.]

Server-side template injection (SSTI) via Jinja2 user-controlled template fragment — Remote code execution and arbitrary file read on the server via Jinja2 sandbox escape techniques; full application compromise. [verified: Same SSTI as findings 0 and 13: user-controlled `fragment` concatenated into Jinja2 Template on line 82 with no sanitization, enabling template injection and potential RCE.]

Path traversal — arbitrary file write via user-controlled path with unbounded body — Attacker can write arbitrary files anywhere on the filesystem (e.g. overwrite application code, write cron jobs, drop SSH authorized_keys), leading to remote code execution or persistent backdoor. [verified: Same path traversal write as findings 10 and 16: user-controlled `name` joined to `BASE_EXPORT_DIR` on line 90 without sanitization, enabling arbitrary file write via directory traversal.]

XXE via external entity resolution in XML parser — Attacker can read arbitrary files from the server filesystem, perform internal network scanning via SSRF, or cause denial of service through entity expansion attacks. [verified: Same XXE as findings 4 and 17: `XMLParser(resolve_entities=True, load_dtd=True, no_network=False)` on line 96 parses attacker-supplied XML with external entity resolution enabled.]

NoSQL injection via user-controlled MongoDB query filter — Attacker can execute arbitrary JavaScript on the MongoDB server (via $where), exfiltrate data through regex-based blind extraction, or bypass query constraints to access unauthorized records. [verified: Same NoSQL injection as findings 5 and 19: user-supplied JSON filter passed directly to `find_one(query)` on line 109, enabling MongoDB operator injection and query manipulation.]

Missing rate limiting on authentication endpoints — Attacker performs unlimited brute-force password guessing and password-reset token enumeration without lockout or throttling [verified: Same as finding [1]: no rate-limiting mechanism exists; all four auth endpoints are reachable without throttling, enabling unlimited brute-force and token-guessing attacks.]

Session cookie missing Secure flag — Session tokens transmitted over plain HTTP can be intercepted via MITM attacks, leading to session hijacking [verified: Same as finding [3]: line 207 sets secure=False on the session cookie with no compensating TLS enforcement, exposing JWT tokens over plaintext HTTP.]

Password reset tokens written to plaintext log file — Attacker with filesystem access reads password-reset tokens from the log and resets any user's password [verified: password_reset_request (line 322) writes the plaintext reset token via json.dumps into storage/mock_outbox/password_resets.log; any filesystem reader can harvest active tokens and reset arbitrary user passwords.]

Missing Rate Limiting on Authentication Endpoints — Credential brute-forcing, account lockout bypass, denial of service via resource exhaustion on auth endpoints. [verified: No rate-limiting middleware, decorator, or in-memory throttle exists anywhere in the codebase (confirmed by search); POST /api/auth/login, /register, /password-reset/request, and /password-reset/confirm are all reachable without any request-limiting control.]

Missing Secure Flag on Session Cookie — Session tokens can be intercepted over unencrypted HTTP, enabling session hijacking via man-in-the-middle attacks. [verified: Line 207 sets secure=False explicitly on the session cookie; no compensating HTTPS redirect or HSTS header is enforced, so the JWT token is transmitted over unencrypted HTTP when the app is accessed without TLS.]

Customer portal self-registration allows arbitrary customer_id association without affiliation verification — An unauthenticated attacker can register as a portal user for any customer in the system, gaining access to that customer's jobs, proof uploads (customer-visible), messages, incidents (customer_summary), and contact details exposed through the API — a cross-tenant data breach against arbitrary customer accounts. [verified: register (line 287) checks only db.get(Customer, payload.customer_id) for existence with no affiliation/invitation verification; after registration, job_query_for_user scopes by user.customer_id, granting immediate cross-tenant data access to the claimed customer's jobs, proofs, and incidents.]

Password reset tokens stored in plaintext log file — An attacker who gains filesystem read access can collect active password reset tokens from the log and take over any user account that has requested a password reset. [verified: Same as finding [12]: line 322 logs the plaintext password-reset token alongside the user email to password_resets.log, enabling account takeover by any actor with filesystem read access.]

Open Redirect in ops after endpoint — Phishing and credential theft by redirecting authenticated users to attacker-controlled sites. [verified: User-controlled `lane` parameter is passed directly to `RedirectResponse(lane)` on line 49 with no URL validation, allowing redirect to arbitrary external sites. The token gate does not validate the redirect target.]

Denial of service via unbounded count parameter in /ops/spool — Attacker with internal token exhausts server memory by requesting a massive count, causing application crash or unavailability [verified: User-controlled `count` parameter on line 57 drives `range(count)` with no upper bound for in-memory list allocation, enabling memory exhaustion and denial of service.]

Reflected XSS via Jinja2 |safe filter in /ops/blurb — Attacker with internal token injects arbitrary JavaScript that executes in the victim's browser context when they visit the crafted URL [verified: Same XSS as finding 6: `card` rendered with `|safe` filter in `HTMLResponse` on line 64, disabling HTML escaping and enabling script injection in a victim's browser.]

Reflected CORS origin with credentials in /ops/origin — Any malicious website can make authenticated cross-origin requests to the /ops/origin endpoint with the victim's cookies/credentials [verified: Same CORS misconfiguration as finding 8: Origin header reflected into `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` on line 74, allowing any origin to make credentialed requests.]

Denial of service via unbounded in-memory list allocation — Attacker can exhaust server memory by requesting a huge count value, causing the application to crash or become unresponsive, denying service to legitimate users. [verified: Same DoS as finding 21: unbounded `count` drives `range(count)` on line 57 for in-memory list creation with no upper limit, enabling memory exhaustion.]

Cross-site scripting (XSS) via Jinja2 |safe filter on user-controlled HTML — Attacker can execute arbitrary JavaScript in the browser of anyone who visits the crafted URL, enabling session theft, credential phishing, or DOM manipulation. [verified: Same XSS as findings 6 and 14: `card` rendered with `|safe` in `HTMLResponse` on line 64, disabling auto-escaping and enabling script injection in victim browsers.]

HTTP Header Injection / CORS Misconfiguration in ops origin endpoint — HTTP response splitting, arbitrary CORS origin with credentials, enabling cross-origin attacks with session cookies. [verified: The endpoint on line 72 reflects the `Origin` request header into `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` and sets `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, allowing any origin to make credentialed cross-origin requests. CRLF header injection is mitigated by modern ASGI but the permissive CORS with credentials is exploitable.]

Weak PRNG used for security-sensitive code generation in /ops/nonce — Generated nonces/codes are predictable, allowing an attacker to guess valid values and bypass any security checks relying on them [verified: `random.choice` (Mersenne Twister) is used on line 93 instead of `secrets.choice` for generating values explicitly named nonces, making outputs predictable if PRNG state is reconstructed from observed values.]

Reflected CORS header with credentials allows cross-origin requests from any origin — Any malicious website can make authenticated cross-origin requests to the ops endpoints, potentially reading sensitive data or performing actions on behalf of authenticated users whose browsers visit the attacker's site. [verified: Same CORS misconfiguration as findings 8 and 23: reflected Origin with credentials on line 74 allows cross-origin credentialed requests from any origin.]

Denial of service via unbounded file upload to filesystem — Attacker can exhaust server disk space by repeatedly uploading large payloads, causing application and potentially system-wide failures due to full disk. [verified: The `/ops/dock` endpoint on line 90 writes the full request body to disk via `target.write_bytes(body)` with no size limit enforcement, allowing an attacker to exhaust disk space through repeated large uploads.]

Weak PRNG used for nonce/code generation in /ops endpoint — An attacker who observes a sequence of generated codes can predict future outputs, compromising any downstream use of these nonces for security purposes (CSRF tokens, transaction IDs, one-time codes). [verified: Same weak PRNG as finding 25: `random.choice` on line 93 instead of `secrets.choice` for generating security-sensitive nonce values, making outputs predictable.]

Missing HTTP Security Headers (HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options) — Users' session cookies may be transmitted over unencrypted HTTP connections (no HSTS enforcement), the SPA frontend is vulnerable to clickjacking attacks (no X-Frame-Options), and browsers may incorrectly MIME-sniff responses leading to XSS or other code execution (no X-Content-Type-Options). [verified: No HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options, or X-Frame-Options headers are set anywhere in the application code; the only middleware added is CORSMiddleware (main.py line 57), and the SPA catch-all route serves index.html without any security headers. The session cookie uses secure=False, compounding the absence of HSTS enforcement.]

Missing CSRF Protection on All State-Changing Endpoints — An attacker can craft malicious websites or emails that, when visited by an authenticated user, silently perform state-changing operations such as creating/deleting jobs, changing job statuses, creating incidents, reordering routes, or modifying user accounts — all within the victim's authorized session context. [verified: The app authenticates via the dispatch_session cookie (set with SameSite=Lax) and accepts it as an alternative to the Authorization header at main.py line ~205, yet contains zero CSRF tokens, Origin/Referer validation, or custom-header checks anywhere in the codebase. SameSite=Lax provides partial mitigation in modern browsers but is not a complete CSRF defense per OWASP guidance.]

Account enumeration via registration endpoint — Attacker enumerates valid user email addresses for targeted phishing, credential stuffing, or password-reset attacks [verified: Same as finding [2]: register endpoint line 213 returns HTTP 409 'Email already registered' vs 422 for other failures, enabling unauthenticated email enumeration.]

User Account Enumeration via Registration Endpoint — Attacker can build a list of valid registered email addresses for targeted phishing or credential-stuffing attacks. [verified: Line 213 returns HTTP 409 'Email already registered' when email exists, vs 422 for invalid customer_id on line 287; an unauthenticated attacker can probe email addresses and observe the distinct status codes.]

Unbounded memory consumption in CSV import — Attacker exhausts server memory by uploading an extremely large CSV file, causing application crash or unavailability [verified: Same as finding [6]: import_csv (line 410) reads the entire upload into memory via await file.read() with no size ceiling, unlike the 10 MB gate on proof uploads.]

CSV formula injection in export endpoints — Attacker injects spreadsheet formulas into CSV exports; when an admin opens the exported file in Excel, arbitrary commands or data exfiltration occurs [verified: Same as finding [0]: csv_response (line 837) delivers customer_summary and internal_notes into CSV output with no formula-character escaping, and IncidentCreate accepts these fields without sanitization.]

Unbounded file upload in CSV import allows memory exhaustion DoS — An authenticated dispatcher or admin can crash the server by uploading an extremely large CSV file, causing denial of service for all users. [verified: import_csv (line 410) calls await file.read() with no size limit; unlike upload_proof (line 384) which enforces a 10 MB cap, an authenticated dispatcher/admin can exhaust server memory with an arbitrarily large CSV.]

CSV Formula Injection in Data Exports — Arbitrary command execution on the machine of any user who opens the exported CSV in a spreadsheet application. [verified: csv_response (line 837) writes DB values via csv.DictWriter with no prefixing of =/+/-/@; incident fields customer_summary and internal_notes flow from user input (IncidentCreate schema) through the database to the CSV sink with zero sanitization.]

CSV formula injection in incident export via unescaped user-controlled text — When an administrator opens the exported CSV in a spreadsheet application, injected formulas can execute arbitrary commands, exfiltrate data, or establish outbound connections from the victim's machine. [verified: Same as findings [0] and [13]: csv_response (line 837) writes incident customer_summary and internal_notes into CSV via DictWriter with no formula-character prefixing, and no sanitization exists in the input path.]

Route CSV export lacks authorization scoping for field_worker role — A field worker can export the complete route schedule for all regions, bypassing the per-worker scoping enforced on the /api/routes listing endpoint and gaining cross-region visibility into other workers' routes, job assignments, and stop orders. [verified: Same root cause as finding [4]: export/routes (line 866) queries all Route rows with only a dispatcher filter (line 868), omitting the field_worker scope (Route.worker_id == user.id) that /api/routes enforces.]

Information disclosure of environment variables and filesystem paths in /ops/trace — Attacker learns internal server paths and environment configuration, aiding further targeted attacks [verified: The endpoint on line 101 exposes `APP_ENV` environment variable and `BASE_EXPORT_DIR` filesystem path in its JSON response, disclosing internal server configuration that aids targeted attacks but has no direct exploitation path.]

Account enumeration via login timing side-channel — Attacker determines which email addresses have accounts by measuring response time differences, enabling targeted attacks [verified: Login line 200-201 short-circuits verify_password (bcrypt) when user is None; when user exists, bcrypt runs with measurable delay, creating a network-observable timing side-channel that leaks account existence.]
